difficultyReason: Three-claim stimulus with a concession-rebuttal frame. The quoted claim is acknowledged by the columnist but then rejected, not endorsed. Trap (A) misreads it as the main conclusion; trap (D) misreads it as supporting that conclusion.
stimulus: Columnist: Some commentators have argued that the rise of remote work will hollow out downtown business districts within a decade. Admittedly, office vacancy rates in several major cities have climbed sharply since remote work became widespread. However, those same districts have seen a surge in residential conversions and new restaurants, and foot traffic on weekends now exceeds pre-pandemic levels. Downtowns are therefore not being hollowed out; they are being transformed.
questionStem: The claim that office vacancy rates in several major cities have climbed sharply since remote work became widespread plays which one of the following roles in the columnist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion that the columnist is defending.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a consideration the columnist concedes but argues does not establish what commentators take it to establish.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is offered as direct support for the conclusion that downtowns are being transformed rather than hollowed out.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of the commentators' position that the columnist endorses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is cited as evidence that foot traffic has returned to pre-pandemic levels.

explanations.correct: The columnist uses 'admittedly' to acknowledge the vacancy data, then uses 'however' to rebut the inference commentators draw from it. That is a conceded consideration the columnist grants but argues is insufficient for the commentators' conclusion.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is that downtowns are being transformed, not hollowed out — signaled by 'therefore.'
explanations.C: The vacancy data would, if anything, cut against the columnist's conclusion; the conversions and foot-traffic data support it.
explanations.D: The columnist explicitly rejects the commentators' conclusion rather than endorsing their supporting premise.
explanations.E: Accurate content, wrong function — it has nothing to do with foot-traffic restoration.

difficultyReason: Four-claim stimulus in which the quoted phrase is a subsidiary conclusion supporting the main one. Students must distinguish it from the main conclusion and from the premises cited for it.
stimulus: Historian: The standard view that the printing press caused the Protestant Reformation overstates technology's role. In the decades before Gutenberg, hand-copied tracts by reformers like Wycliffe and Hus circulated widely throughout Europe and provoked real ecclesiastical crises. So the ideas driving the Reformation were already gaining traction without mechanical reproduction. The press accelerated a process that was underway, rather than initiating one.
questionStem: The claim that the ideas driving the Reformation were already gaining traction without mechanical reproduction plays which one of the following roles in the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a premise offered in direct support of the claim that hand-copied tracts circulated widely before Gutenberg.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is an intermediate conclusion drawn from evidence about pre-Gutenberg tracts and used to support the historian's main claim about the press's role.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a view the historian attributes to opponents in order to rebut it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is background context that orients the reader before the argument begins.

explanations.correct: The claim is drawn ('so') from the evidence about Wycliffe and Hus and is then used to support the final claim that the press accelerated rather than initiated the Reformation. It is both conclusion and premise — an intermediate conclusion.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the final sentence, about the press accelerating rather than initiating.
explanations.B: Reverses the support relation — the tracts claim supports the traction claim, not the other way around.
explanations.D: The historian endorses the claim; it is not attributed to opponents.
explanations.E: It is argumentatively load-bearing, not scene-setting.

difficultyReason: Analogy-based argument where the quoted phrase is a premise of the analogy. Students must distinguish it from the main conclusion about the policy and from stand-alone background.
stimulus: Policy analyst: Some officials insist that the city's new congestion-pricing plan will fail because drivers will simply shift to side streets. But a comparable pricing plan in Stockholm produced a durable 20 percent reduction in total vehicle miles within two years. Since Stockholm's street grid, commuter patterns, and driver demographics closely resemble ours, we should expect a similar reduction here. The officials' pessimism is therefore unfounded.
questionStem: The claim that a comparable pricing plan in Stockholm produced a durable 20 percent reduction in total vehicle miles within two years plays which one of the following roles in the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion the analyst defends.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the basis for an analogy from which the analyst infers the expected effect of the city's plan.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a view the analyst attributes to officials in order to reject it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is offered as evidence that Stockholm's street grid resembles the city's.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a concession the analyst makes to critics before rebutting them.

explanations.correct: The analyst compares the city to Stockholm and uses Stockholm's observed reduction as the comparator in the analogy. The similarity premises then license projecting Stockholm's result onto the city.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is that officials' pessimism is unfounded — the final sentence.
explanations.C: The analyst endorses Stockholm's result rather than attributing it to officials.
explanations.D: Reverses the support relation — the grid similarity supports the projection, not the other way around.
explanations.E: The analyst isn't conceding ground; the Stockholm datum anchors the argument.

difficultyReason: Concession-rebuttal structure in a medical context. The quoted phrase is a consideration the physician raises in order to reject its implications. Trap (C) misreads as endorsed support; trap (D) misreads as the conclusion itself.
stimulus: Physician: Critics of the new screening guidelines argue that fewer screenings will mean more late-stage diagnoses. It is true that screening programs sometimes detect cancers at earlier stages than they would otherwise be found. Nevertheless, the new guidelines will not increase late-stage diagnoses overall, because the cancers most likely to be flagged by early screening are slow-growing types that rarely progress to serious disease in the interval between recommended screenings.
questionStem: The claim that screening programs sometimes detect cancers at earlier stages than they would otherwise be found plays which one of the following roles in the physician's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the physician's argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a claim whose truth the physician grants but whose critic-favored inference the physician denies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is evidence directly supporting the conclusion that late-stage diagnoses will not rise under the new guidelines.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the critics' main conclusion, which the physician argues against.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an intermediate conclusion drawn from data about slow-growing cancers.

explanations.correct: The physician uses 'it is true that ... nevertheless' to grant the factual claim while denying the critics' inference from it. That is a conceded consideration.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is that the new guidelines will not increase late-stage diagnoses.
explanations.C: If anything, this claim cuts against the physician's conclusion; the slow-growing-cancer point is what supports it.
explanations.D: The critics' conclusion is that late-stage diagnoses will rise; the quoted claim is a premise for that conclusion, not the conclusion itself.
explanations.E: No evidence for this claim is supplied in the stimulus.

difficultyReason: Two-level argument in linguistics. The quoted claim is an intermediate conclusion: supported by the corpus observation and used to support the main claim about adult learners.
stimulus: Linguist: A recent corpus study found that young children use grammatical constructions they have never heard from caregivers. It follows that children are not learning grammar simply by imitating adult speech. If they were, their output would be bounded by the constructions available to them as input. Therefore adult language learners, who rely more heavily on explicit imitation, face a genuinely different cognitive task from children.
questionStem: The claim that children are not learning grammar simply by imitating adult speech plays which one of the following roles in the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is offered as background context that does not bear on the main conclusion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a view the linguist attributes to others and rejects.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a conclusion for which the corpus observation is offered as support, and which in turn is used to support the argument's main claim about adult learners.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a premise for the corpus observation that precedes it.

explanations.correct: 'It follows that' signals that this claim is concluded from the corpus observation. The final sentence, signaled by 'therefore,' uses it to support the claim about adult learners. It is therefore an intermediate conclusion.
explanations.A: The main conclusion concerns adult learners, reached in the final sentence.
explanations.C: The linguist endorses the claim rather than attributing it to others.
explanations.E: Reverses the support relation — the corpus observation supports this claim, not the other way around.

difficultyReason: Environmental-science argument with explicit concession signal. The quoted claim is acknowledged but rejected as decisive; distinguishing it from a supporting premise is the test.
stimulus: Environmentalist: Advocates of a wetland-restoration project near our river claim that it will substantially reduce downstream flooding. Granted, wetlands in general can absorb significant volumes of floodwater during storm surges. However, the site proposed for restoration lies upstream of only a small fraction of the tributaries that contribute to our river's flood peaks. The project is therefore unlikely to produce the broad flood reduction its advocates promise.
questionStem: The claim that wetlands in general can absorb significant volumes of floodwater during storm surges plays which one of the following roles in the environmentalist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is evidence offered directly in support of the conclusion that the project is unlikely to produce broad flood reduction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a claim whose truth the environmentalist grants but whose relevance to the specific project the environmentalist disputes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is an intermediate conclusion supported by evidence about the project site.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the advocates' main conclusion, which the environmentalist rejects.

explanations.correct: 'Granted ... however' marks a conceded consideration. The environmentalist accepts that wetlands generally absorb floodwater but argues that this general fact does not carry the weight the advocates want for the specific site.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is that the project is unlikely to produce broad flood reduction.
explanations.B: The absorption capability, if anything, cuts the other way; the tributary point supports the environmentalist's conclusion.
explanations.D: No evidence is offered for this general claim; the environmentalist simply grants it.
explanations.E: The advocates' conclusion is about this project specifically, not about wetlands in general.

difficultyReason: Ethics argument with an analogy premise. Students must distinguish a premise of the comparison from the main evaluative conclusion it supports.
stimulus: Ethicist: When a pharmacist mistakenly dispenses the wrong medication and a patient is harmed, we rightly hold the pharmacist morally responsible, even if the mistake was inadvertent. An autonomous vehicle's decision algorithm sorts among options and chooses actions in much the way a pharmacist sorts and selects from available drugs. Thus, when an autonomous vehicle inadvertently causes harm, the company that designed its algorithm bears genuine moral responsibility.
questionStem: The claim that when a pharmacist mistakenly dispenses the wrong medication and a patient is harmed, we rightly hold the pharmacist morally responsible, even if the mistake was inadvertent, plays which one of the following roles in the ethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the ethicist's argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is one term of an analogy, offered to support the conclusion about the company that designed the algorithm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a view the ethicist attributes to others in order to rebut it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is an intermediate conclusion drawn from the claim about autonomous vehicles.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a concession to critics of algorithmic accountability.

explanations.correct: The ethicist uses the pharmacist case as the familiar term in an analogy and then, by comparing the algorithm's decision-making to the pharmacist's, draws the conclusion about the company's moral responsibility.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is about the company's moral responsibility, signaled by 'thus.'
explanations.C: The ethicist endorses, not rejects, the pharmacist judgment.
explanations.D: No evidence is offered for the pharmacist claim; it is a starting premise.
explanations.E: Nothing in the stimulus presents the claim as a concession; it is affirmed.

difficultyReason: Arts-criticism stimulus with a subsidiary conclusion supporting the main aesthetic claim. Trap (A) confuses the subsidiary conclusion with the main one; trap (C) describes a role not played.
stimulus: Critic: Several reviewers have praised the novel's intricate nested timelines as its principal achievement. But the nested structure only works because each timeline ends on a moment of specific, quiet loss, and those losses echo one another. So it is the emotional architecture, not the temporal puzzle, that does the real work. The novel's power is therefore best understood as a triumph of sentiment, not of form.
questionStem: The claim that it is the emotional architecture, not the temporal puzzle, that does the real work plays which one of the following roles in the critic's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the critic's argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a subsidiary conclusion drawn from observations about the timelines and their endings, and it in turn supports the final claim about the novel's power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a view the critic attributes to reviewers in order to reject it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is offered as direct support for the claim that several reviewers have praised the nested timelines.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a concession the critic makes before turning to the main argument.

explanations.correct: The claim is drawn ('so') from observations about the matched endings and is then used to support the final sentence's verdict about where the novel's power lies. It is a subsidiary conclusion.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the final sentence about the novel's power.
explanations.C: The critic endorses this claim rather than attributing it to reviewers.
explanations.D: Reverses the support relation — the timeline-endings observation supports this claim, not the other way around.
explanations.E: The critic advances, rather than concedes, this claim.

difficultyReason: Legal-reasoning stimulus with concession structure. The quoted claim is a consideration the professor raises only to argue it does not entail the critics' conclusion.
stimulus: Law professor: Critics of the new evidence rule argue that it will let juries hear too much prejudicial testimony. To be sure, the rule permits a broader range of character evidence than the previous standard allowed. But trial judges under the new rule retain the same discretion to exclude evidence whose probative value is outweighed by its prejudicial effect. Thus the critics' worry is overstated; the practical scope of admissible prejudicial testimony will not expand appreciably.
questionStem: The claim that the rule permits a broader range of character evidence than the previous standard allowed plays which one of the following roles in the professor's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the professor's argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a factual concession that the professor grants to critics but argues does not support the conclusion the critics draw from it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is offered as direct support for the conclusion that the practical scope of admissible prejudicial testimony will not expand appreciably.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a view the professor attributes to judges rather than to critics.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an intermediate conclusion supported by the claim about judges' discretion.

explanations.correct: 'To be sure ... but' frames a conceded consideration. The professor grants the claim and then argues, via the discretion point, that the critics' worry does not follow from it.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is that the critics' worry is overstated.
explanations.C: This claim actually seems to favor the critics; the discretion claim is what supports the professor's conclusion.
explanations.D: The professor attributes the broader worry to critics, not this factual observation to judges.
explanations.E: No evidence is offered for this claim; it is simply granted.

difficultyReason: Technology-policy argument whose quoted claim is a subsidiary conclusion bridging premises about outages to the main claim about regulation. Trap (D) reverses the support direction; trap (E) mislabels as a concession.
stimulus: Technologist: Over the past decade, outages at large cloud providers have caused cascading failures across banks, hospitals, and transit systems. Each incident traces back to configuration errors at a single provider that simultaneously handled workloads for all the affected sectors. So the concentration of critical services in a few providers is itself a public-safety problem. Regulators should therefore require large providers to support standardized interoperability so that customers can fail over to competitors during outages.
questionStem: The claim that the concentration of critical services in a few providers is itself a public-safety problem plays which one of the following roles in the technologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the technologist's argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a claim drawn from the pattern of outages described, and it is in turn used to support the call for standardized interoperability.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is background context unrelated to the regulatory recommendation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a premise offered in direct support of the claim that configuration errors caused the outages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a concession the technologist makes to defenders of the current cloud market before rejecting their view.

explanations.correct: 'So' marks this claim as concluded from the outage pattern, and 'therefore' in the final sentence uses it to support the regulatory recommendation. That double role is characteristic of an intermediate conclusion.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the regulatory recommendation in the final sentence.
explanations.C: It is the pivot of the argument, not peripheral context.
explanations.D: Reverses the support relation — the configuration-error observation supports this claim, not the other way around.
explanations.E: The technologist advances, rather than concedes, the claim.
